title: How Movie Magic Brought Rotta the Hutt and Old-School Effects to 'The Mandalorian and Grogu'
summary:
How do you make giant walking machines and a muscly space slug look real on screen? Hal Hickel, an animation supervisor at the special-effects company Industrial Light & Magic, or ILM, shared some secrets from "The Mandalorian and Grogu" at the View Conference in Turin, Italy, on Thursday.

Hickel said he kept asking one question: "What would Phil do?" He meant Phil Tippett, a pioneer of stop-motion, a technique where puppets are moved a tiny bit at a time and photographed frame by frame. Tippett's work on the original "Star Wars" movies inspired much of the new film.

For the opening battle, the team made the giant AT-AT walkers move even more slowly to show how heavy they are. A full-sized set even stretched through a walker's neck into its movable head. For the smaller AT-RT, animators studied ostriches, then used that movement to control a mechanical rig carrying the actors.

Rotta the Hutt, voiced by Jeremy Allen White, needed to move like a powerful fighter. ILM studied elephant seals and sumo wrestlers. But director Jon Favreau felt the first design "didn't feel Hutt-y enough," so the team changed Rotta's face and colors to look more like his father, Jabba. Because Rotta talks so much, the filmmakers had him speak English so younger viewers would not have to read lots of subtitles. One scene, with Grogu asleep on Rotta's chest, was a tribute to the animated film "My Neighbor Totoro."

The movie also includes a real stop-motion fight between two giant droids, made with Tippett's animators. Hickel even moved a puppet himself. He said doing stop-motion on a "Star Wars" film "will probably be forever the pinnacle of my career."
why_it_matters: It shows how filmmakers blend old-fashioned handmade techniques with modern computer effects to make movie worlds feel real.

background_read: Visual effects, or VFX, are images created or changed by artists so that things impossible to film for real can appear on screen.
Industrial Light & Magic is a special-effects company that has worked on Star Wars films since the original movies.
Before computer graphics became common, many movie creatures were brought to life with stop-motion puppets photographed one frame at a time.
Today filmmakers often mix computer animation with real sets and machines so scenes feel more solid and believable.
